body_ar:
لله تعالى الأسماء الحسنى والصفات العلا، وقد أثبت أهل السنة لله ما أثبته لنفسه من الصفات والأسماء كما يليق بجلاله، وذموا من ألحد في أسماء الله أو نفاها، وكذلك صفاته.
إثبات أسماء الله الحسنى.
قال الشيخ حفظه الله: [ أسماؤه الحسنى على الصفات دلت فذلت أوجه النفاة ......].
أصل اشتقاق الاسم:
والاسم مختلف فيه: فقيل: هو مشتق من السمو؛ لأنه يسمو به مسماه فيرفعه من حالة المجهولية إلى المعلومية فيعرف به. وقيل: مشتق من السمة؛ لأنه علامة على مسماه، وقد اختلف الكوفيون والبصريون فيه: فقال البصريون: أصله (سمو) كقنو فحذفت لامه وعرضت الهاء بهمزة الوصل مثل ابن، فإن همزة الوصل التي فيه عوض من اللام وأصله بنو وهكذا. وقال الكوفيون: أصله (وسم) من السمة التي هي العلامة، ففاء الكلمة هي المحذوفة وعوض منها همزة الوصل. لكن مذهب البصريين أصح؛ لأننا نقول: أسماء ولا نقول: أوسام، ونقول: سمي ولا نقول: وُسَيم، ونقول: سميت ابني زيداً، ولا نقول: وسمت ابني زيداً ، وهذا الذي يقول فيه أحدهم: اشتق الاسم من سما البصريُ واشتقه من وسم الكوفـيُ والمذهب المقدم الجليّ دليله الأسماء والـسـميُّ
body_en:
*[Site synopsis]* To God, exalted is He, belong the most beautiful names and the most exalted attributes. The People of the Sunnah have affirmed for God what He affirmed for Himself of attributes and names, in the manner that befits His majesty, and they have censured whoever deviates concerning God's names or denies them, and likewise His attributes.

## Affirming God's most beautiful names

The Sheikh, may God preserve him, said:

*[His most beautiful names point to the attributes, and so the faces of the deniers were humbled ……]*

## The derivation of the word "name"

The word "name" (ism) is disputed. It is said that it is derived from sumuww, elevation, because that which is named is elevated by it, so that it raises it from the condition of being unknown to the condition of being known, and it comes to be known by it. And it is said that it is derived from simah, a mark, because it is a mark upon that which is named.

The Kufans and the Basrans differed over it. The Basrans said: its root is s-m-w, on the pattern of qinw; its final radical was dropped and compensated for by the conjunctive hamzah, as in ibn — for the conjunctive hamzah in that word is a substitute for the final radical, its root being banaw, and so on. The Kufans said: its root is w-s-m, from simah, which is the mark; so it is the first radical of the word that was dropped, and the conjunctive hamzah was put in its place.

But the position of the Basrans is the sounder, because we say asmāʾ and we do not say awsām; and we say sumayy and we do not say wusaym; and we say "I named my son Zayd" (sammaytu) and we do not say "I marked my son Zayd" (wasamtu). This is what one of them expressed when he said:

*The Basran derived the noun from samā, and the Kufan derived it from wasama; and the position given precedence is the manifest one — its evidence is asmāʾ and sumayy.*

flags.context: فقال البصريون: أصله (سمو) كقنو فحذفت لامه وعرضت الهاء بهمزة الوصل مثل ابن
options: read as وعُوِّض عنها بهمزة الوصل — 'and compensated for by the conjunctive hamzah', which is what the next clause states in so many words
leave the text as served and mark it unintelligible
flags.note: Source corruption, style guide section 11. 'عرضت الهاء' does not parse here: no hā' is under discussion, and the clause that immediately follows ('for the conjunctive hamzah in it is a substitute for the final radical') states the compensation doctrine explicitly. Almost certainly a transcription error for a form of عوّض. The Arabic is preserved exactly as served in body_ar and NOT corrected; the English renders the only reading the passage admits and this flag records the defect for the Sheikh's office.

options: retain both diminutives untranslated with the Arabic in brackets
gloss them as 'little name' and 'little mark'
flags.note: The argument is a morphological one and works only on the Arabic forms; glossing them into English destroys the evidence it rests on. The forms are kept as they stand and the reader is given the shape of the argument rather than a rendering of the words.

flags.note: 'النفاة' is the same polemical target as al-Muʿaṭṭilah elsewhere in this run. The line is quoted and then abandoned — the record turns at once to the lexical question and never returns to it — so the referent is left as the Arabic leaves it.

translator_notes: One of a run of fourteen records, IDs 734-747, the series 'The Names and Attributes', all built to the same template and all excerpts. Each carries a site-written synopsis, then a section heading, then the opening formula and the first lines of a lesson, and then breaks off on an ellipsis; the full text sits behind a .doc download in the /medias/doc/esmawesivat-* series, numbered 1 to 14 in the same order as the IDs.

The source's final line, 'تحميل المادة' ('download the material'), is the label of a download link in the page furniture, not part of the text. It is recorded as source_download_link and omitted from body_ar and body_en.

This record does carry a CMS timestamp in a .create_date span (10 May 2011, within a 28-minute window shared by the whole run 738-747). That is a bulk-upload timestamp for the series, not the date the lesson was given. Record 737, translated in an earlier wave, reports no date for this run; the timestamp is in fact present in the page and should be backfilled there.

Creedal material. Per style guide section 8, the vocabulary of divine attributes is not the vocabulary of the five legal rulings, and the five-rulings mapping is not applied to any predicate of God in this record.

Unusually for this run, the excerpt does not end on the source's own ellipsis: it runs to the end of a line of verse and simply stops. The break is no less abrupt for that — the creedal claim announced in the heading is never argued, and the whole of the surviving text is a lexical digression on the etymology of the word 'name'. Marked critical_for_display.

The two lines of verse at the close are rendered as prose in italics per style guide section 4, with no attempt at rhyme; the Arabic is retained in the facing pane. The Sheikh attributes them only to 'one of them' and names no poet, so the English names none.
Root letters are given in the English as s-m-w and w-s-m rather than transliterated as words, because the point at issue is which consonant was dropped.
'مذهب' here means a grammarians' school position, not a madhhab in the legal sense, and is rendered 'position' to keep the two apart.
